551.event_title: Idi Amin expels Uganda's Asian community
551.event: On 4 August 1972 Uganda's military ruler Idi Amin ordered the country's Asian population, most of them of Indian and Pakistani descent, to leave within 90 days, claiming they were sabotaging the economy. Tens of thousands were forced out, allowed to take only what they could carry, and received no compensation for their homes and businesses. The community had played a central role in Uganda's commerce, and the expulsion contributed to the country's economic decline in the 1970s.
551.explanation: A ruler used the power of the state to strip a whole community of its livelihood and property, causing suffering that lasted for years.
551.tie_back: The kural says a king who makes a practice of harassing his people and doing injustice is crueller than a murderer, and Amin's expulsion order harmed tens of thousands for the rest of their lives.
551._accuracy_note: A strong case of state harassment driven partly by desire to seize wealth, matching Parimelazhagar's reading, though it targeted one community rather than all subjects.

552.event_title: Charles I's forced loan and the Five Knights' Case
552.event: Unable to get the taxes he wanted from Parliament, Charles I demanded a forced loan from his subjects in 1626-27 and had more than 70 gentlemen who refused to pay imprisoned. Five of them, led by Sir Thomas Darnel, sought release through the courts in the Five Knights' Case of 1627, but the judges refused bail. In 1628 Parliament answered with the Petition of Right, which declared that no one should be taxed without Parliament's consent or imprisoned without cause shown.
552.explanation: The king called his demand a loan, but because refusal meant prison it was really taking by force.
552.tie_back: The kural says that when a ruler holding the sceptre asks his subjects for money it is like a robber with a spear saying 'hand it over', which is exactly how Charles I's forced loan worked.
552._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: a royal 'request' for money backed by the threat of punishment, which is the kural's exact image.

553.event_title: Emperor Huizong's neglect of government and the fall of Kaifeng
553.event: Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty, who reigned from 1100, is remembered as a gifted painter, calligrapher and patron of the arts, and Britannica records that he sought escape from affairs of state in the pleasures of arts and letters. When the Jurchen invaded he abdicated in favour of his son in 1125-26. The Jurchen then captured the capital, Kaifeng, and took both Huizong and his son into captivity, ending the Northern Song dynasty in 1127.
553.explanation: An emperor absorbed in the arts rather than the daily business of ruling saw his realm decline and finally fall.
553.tie_back: The kural warns that a king who does not look into wrongs every day and give justice will see his country decline day by day, as Huizong's did.
553._accuracy_note: A good fit for daily neglect of government leading to ruin, though outside invasion, not only misrule, brought about the fall.

554.event_title: Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes
554.event: In October 1685 Louis XIV issued the Edict of Fontainebleau, revoking the Edict of Nantes that had given French Protestants (Huguenots) religious toleration since 1598. Although emigration was forbidden, at least 200,000 Huguenots fled to the Netherlands, England, Prussia, America and elsewhere over the following years. Many were skilled craftsmen and merchants, and their departure strengthened the economies of France's rivals while weakening France's own.
554.explanation: A single unjust decree drove away a large and productive part of the population and with it much of the country's skill and wealth.
554.tie_back: The kural says a king who bends justice without thinking of the consequences loses wealth and people together, and the revocation did exactly that.
554._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: an unjust act that cost the kingdom both its people and the wealth they would have produced.

555.event_title: The Duke of Alba's Tenth Penny and the Dutch Revolt
555.place: The Low Countries (now the Netherlands and Belgium)
555.event: Sent by Philip II of Spain to govern the Netherlands, the Duke of Alba ruled through a special tribunal, the Council of Troubles, and in 1569 announced a permanent ten per cent sales tax, the Tenth Penny. The tax united Catholics and Protestants against Spanish rule. When rebels seized the port of Brielle on 1 April 1572 other towns joined the revolt, and Alba left the Netherlands in 1573 without having restored control.
555.explanation: The suffering caused by harsh rule and heavy taxation turned the population against the crown and began the long process by which Spain lost its richest provinces.
555.tie_back: The kural says the tears of people who can no longer bear their suffering are the weapon that wears away an oppressive ruler's wealth, and the revolt against Alba wore away Spain's hold on the Netherlands.
555._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of oppression turning into the oppressor's loss, though the revolt also had religious and political causes beyond the people's distress.

556.event_title: Stalin's body is removed from Lenin's Mausoleum
556.event: After Stalin's death in 1953 his embalmed body was placed beside Lenin's in the mausoleum on Red Square. During the de-Stalinization campaign led by Nikita Khrushchev, the body was removed on 31 October 1961 and reburied by the Kremlin Wall. The same year the city of Stalingrad was renamed Volgograd.
556.explanation: Within a decade of his death, the honours given to one of history's most feared rulers were being taken down by his own successors.
556.tie_back: The kural says just rule is what makes a king's fame last and that without it his glory will not endure, and the removal of Stalin from the mausoleum shows such glory fading.
556._accuracy_note: A clear example of a tyrant's glory being undone, though the fame of harsh rulers can also persist, so it shows one side of the kural.

557.event_title: Haile Selassie's government and the Wollo famine
557.event: During a drought in 1972-73, famine struck the province of Wollo in northern Ethiopia, and tens of thousands of people died. The imperial government of Haile Selassie tried to conceal the famine, and its denial became an international scandal after it was exposed in a British television documentary. Famine, unemployment and political stagnation fed the unrest that led army officers to depose the emperor on 12 September 1974.
557.explanation: The lack of care from the ruler turned a natural drought into a human disaster and cost him his throne.
557.tie_back: The kural says a king's lack of kindness is to his people what drought is to the world, and in Wollo the two came together.
557._accuracy_note: A strong fit: a ruler's indifference compounded an actual drought, though the famine had several causes.

558.event: After winning the civil war, the dictator Lucius Cornelius Sulla posted public lists of people declared outlaws, and the property of those named was confiscated and sold, often cheaply to his friends and supporters. Britannica describes the victims as some 520 wealthy opponents whose property went to Sulla's veterans, and their sons and grandsons were barred from public office. Ancient writers report that some people were added to the lists simply because others wanted their estates.
558.explanation: Under Sulla's rule owning property became a danger in itself, since wealth could put a person's name on the lists.
558.tie_back: The kural says that under an unjust ruler having wealth brings more misery than having nothing, and the proscriptions made riches a reason to be targeted.
558._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the paradox that under tyranny the rich suffer most, matching Parimelazhagar's gloss closely.

559.event_title: Soviet irrigation schemes dry up the Aral Sea
559.place: Aral Sea, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan (then Soviet Union)
559.event: Soviet planners diverted almost all the water of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton fields in Central Asia, and from the 1960s the Aral Sea, which has no outlet, began to shrink rapidly. By the late 1980s it had split into separate northern and southern seas, rising salinity had destroyed its fishery, and dust from the exposed seabed was degrading farmland. NASA reports that the loss of the water made the region's winters colder and its summers hotter.
559.explanation: Decisions made by a distant government without regard for the people of the region changed their very climate and ruined their livelihoods.
559.tie_back: The kural says that when a ruler rules against justice the seasons go wrong and the rain fails, and Kalaignar's reading of the neglect of water works fits the Aral Sea's fate.
559._accuracy_note: Next-best: a real case of misgovernment upsetting water and seasons, but it was central planning rather than deliberate cruelty, and the kural's classical sense of failing rain is cosmic.

560.event_title: The Nazi book burnings and the purge of German universities
560.place: Berlin and university towns across Germany
560.event: On 7 April 1933 the new Nazi government issued the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, which led to the dismissal of Jewish and politically undesirable university teachers, over 1,100 of them by 1935. On 10 May 1933 pro-Nazi student groups burned books by Jewish, pacifist and left-wing authors in university towns, with some 20,000 volumes burned before a crowd of about 40,000 on Berlin's Opernplatz.
560.explanation: When the state stopped protecting scholars and learning, Germany's universities lost much of the knowledge they had been built to keep.
560.tie_back: The kural warns that when the guardian of the land fails to protect it the learned forget their texts, and the burnings and dismissals of 1933 drove learning out of German universities.
560._accuracy_note: Fits the second half of the kural (learning abandoned under bad rule) but not the first (the cows' yield), and the kural's 'learned' are specifically ritual scholars.
